newsitem.title: USA: Clinton begins second term with modest agenda.
newsitem.headline: Clinton begins second term with modest agenda.

text.p: At Monday's inauguration, Bill Clinton will receive a gift no Democratic president has enjoyed in half a century: a second full term in which to advance his agenda for the nation.

But apart from the goal of balancing the federal budget, scholars and analysts describe that agenda -- laid down in bite-sized morsels during the 1996 election campaign -- as modest at best and a far cry from the ambitions Clinton brought to Washington four years ago.

"When he came into office, Clinton was filled with the idea of himself as a visionary leader on a grand scale like Franklin Roosevelt," said University of New Orleans historian Douglas Brinkley. Roosevelt was the last Democrat elected to a second full term, which he began in 1937.

"It is almost refreshing that the so-called 'vision thing' is being put on hold," Brinkley said. "What you are getting is a pragmatist who is willing ... to roll up his shirtsleeves and get down to hard bipartisan negotiating."
Roosevelt is legendary as the president who led America out of the Great Depression of the 1930s with a wave of New Deal legislation, and for his leadership in World War II.
In comparison, analysts said many of Clinton's ideas for his second term seem narrow, specific and modest, although they note he is governing at a much less momentous time.

During the campaign, he offered a series of small, low-cost initiatives, such as promoting community policing and school uniforms or expanding the law to give workerstime off for parent-teacher meetings and doctors appointments.
Speaking last month to the Democratic Leadership Council, a group of moderates within his party, Clinton laid out his broader goals, with balancing the budget first on his list.
Getting the federal goverment's finances back in the black would be no mean feat: it is an achievement that has eluded every president since Richard Nixon pulled it off in 1969.

But having seen the electorate limit his powers by leaving control of Congress with the Republicans, Clinton can only balance the budget -- or do most anything else -- by working with the opposing party.
That one fact, analysts said, is the clearest explanation for the limited and centrist nature of his agenda.

"The president is strong enough to protect his priorities; he may be strong enough to initiate small incremental policies ... that gain Republican support, but we're not going to see any big fix," said Georgetown University's Stephen Wayne.

Clinton has identified several other goals including improving education, reforming welfare, cutting down on crime and youth violence, and helping people juggle their responsibilities at work and at home.
Historian Brinkley described this as an agenda of trimming and pruning existing programmes and therefore unlikely to make Clinton's second term one that will stand out in history.

"It is one thing when you are trying to create something new and bold, and another when the job that you are trying to do is to restructure something that already exists," he said. "People years from now are not going to say, 'hey Clinton did a great job of restructuring education, of trimming welfare.'"
Clinton spent little time on foreign policy during the campaign but, if he follows the pattern of past presidents, he may place greater emphasis on it during his second term.

Officials cite six strategic goals: building an undivided, peaceful Europe; cementing America's role in the Asia-Pacific region; bringing peace to flashpoints like the Middle East and Northern Ireland; fighting terrorism; maintaining military and diplomatic strength and building an open global economy.
"He forsees an active foreign policy agenda, both for our country and for himself," Samuel Berger, Clinton's newly named national security adviser, said over the weekend.

In any case, time is short for Clinton to put his ideas into practice. Although his term runs until noon on January 20, 2001, his power will begin to wane long before as attentions begin to shift toward the contest to succeed him.

Brookings Institution scholar Stephen Hess said 1997 may be Clinton's best chance for his domestic agenda, noting that attention will shift to the mid-term congressional elections in 1998 and then to the fight for the White House in 2000.
"Second terms have generally been considered like an hour glass, with the sand running out," Hess said.
